sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Introduces the technical brief by explaining that women in high-prevalence settings still acquire HIV during pregnancy and breastfeeding, raising the risk of transmission to infants. It notes established prevention measures and proposes oral PrEP as a complement, then lists the brief's aims.

sections.extract: In many countries with high-prevalence generalized HIV epidemics, women continue to acquire HIV during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Women who become infected during this time also risk transmitting HIV to their infants. Incident HIV infection during pregnancy and breastfeeding contributes to a significant proportion of infants with HIV in very high incidence settings, and is of public health relevance for antenatal

sections.title: What is PrEP?

summary.text: Defines PrEP as daily oral TDF or TDF/FTC taken to prevent HIV acquisition by HIV-negative people.

sections.extract: PrEP is the use of daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or co-formulated TDF/emtricitabine (TDF/FTC) to prevent HIV acquisition. PrEP has been shown to be effective in a wide range of HIV-negative populations.

sections.title: WHO recommendation on PrEP

summary.text: Outlines WHO's 2015 recommendation that oral TDF-containing PrEP be offered to people at substantial HIV risk and how the 2016 consolidated guidelines addressed its use in pregnancy and breastfeeding. It notes that the benefits of preventing maternal HIV and mother-to-child transmission were judged to outweigh potential risks of fetal and infant drug exposure.

sections.extract: In 2015, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended that oral PrEP containing TDF be offered as an additional prevention choice for people at substantial risk1 of HIV infection, as part of combination HIV prevention approaches (1). sections.title: Why offer PrEP to pregnant and breastfeeding women?

summary.text: Explains why pregnant and breastfeeding women in high-incidence settings face increased HIV risk, with a figure listing biological and behavioural factors. It also summarises WHO recommendations on antenatal HIV testing, retesting and partner testing as part of prevention.

sections.extract: Pregnant and breastfeeding women living in settings where HIV incidence is greater than three per 100 person–years, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, often remain at substantial and increased risk of HIV acquisition during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Biological factors increase susceptibility, and social and behavioural factors may increase exposure to HIV infection (Figure 1). Pregnant and breastfeeding women

sections.title: PrEP safety during pregnancy and breastfeeding

summary.text: Reviews evidence on the safety of PrEP during pregnancy and breastfeeding, drawing on a 2016 WHO systematic review of TDF use in HIV-positive and HIV-negative women. It reports that few adverse pregnancy, birth or infant outcomes were linked to TDF, and discusses data on drug levels in breast milk and infant bone and renal effects. It concludes that PrEP can be used in pregnancy and breastfeeding and as part of safer conception.

sections.extract: The 2016 WHO guidelines state that there is no safety-related rationale for disallowing or discontinuing PrEP use during pregnancy and breastfeeding for HIV-negative women who are receiving PrEP and remain at risk of HIV acquisition (1). sections.title: Providing PrEP to women who would most benefit

summary.text: Describes three situations in which HIV-negative pregnant or breastfeeding women may be offered PrEP, together with testing, adherence counselling, monitoring and other prevention options.

sections.extract: Although there is limited experience with the use of PrEP in antenatal and postnatal care services, it is an important new HIV prevention method to consider, particularly for high-burden settings where women remain at significant HIV risk. sections.title: PrEP as part of PMTCT in settings of high HIV incidence

summary.text: Describes how PrEP can be added to comprehensive HIV prevention in antenatal and postnatal care where HIV incidence is high, setting out eight elements of such a package in a box. The elements include repeat testing, partner testing and referral, condoms, STI screening and risk counselling. It also discusses risk assessment tools while cautioning that they should not be used to deny PrEP to women who request it.

sections.extract: For high burden settings and for populations with high HIV incidence in low burden settings, all HIV-negative women should be offered prevention interventions at antenatal and postnatal visits (Box 1). In addition, PrEP could be offered as part of an enhanced comprehensive HIV prevention approach in selected sites where women experience ongoing high HIV incidence. sections.title: PrEP for safer conception

summary.text: Discusses offering PrEP for safer conception to HIV-negative women whose partners have unknown status or are not virally suppressed, stressing that the decision rests with the woman. A Kenyan risk assessment scoring tool for pregnant women is shown as an example.

sections.extract: HIV-negative women in high prevalence settings remain at high HIV risk during the period of conception when their partners are of unknown status, or their partners are living with HIV and are either (a) not on ART or (b) are not virally suppressed (including partners recently starting ART, whose full viral suppression may take up to six months). sections.title: Monitoring PrEP use by pregnant and breastfeeding women

summary.text: Sets out how mother and infant outcomes should be actively monitored when PrEP is used in pregnancy and breastfeeding, covering maternal toxicity, adverse birth outcomes and infant growth and development. It also suggests integrating PrEP indicators into existing drug toxicity surveillance and continuity of PrEP services.

sections.extract: Although the currently available data are reassuring regarding the safety of PrEP during pregnancy and breastfeeding, active surveillance of mother and infant outcomes during PrEP use in pregnancy and breastfeeding should be part of a PrEP programme. sections.title: Summary of issues and considerations

summary.text: A summary table of issues and considerations for PrEP use, covering pregnancy and breastfeeding, desire to conceive, family planning, gender-based violence, sex workers and adolescent girls.

sections.extract: Issues Considerations Pregnancy and breastfeeding PrEP can be started or continued during pregnancy and breastfeeding in women at substantial risk of HIV acquisition. A range of interventions should be offered to HIV-negative women in pregnancy and breastfeeding to prevent and detect incident HIV. sections.title: Key messages

summary.text: Lists key messages of the brief, including that PrEP is safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding, should be part of a comprehensive prevention package, and depends on adherence. It also covers disclosure, changing periods of risk, compatibility with hormonal contraception and cost-effectiveness.

sections.extract: • PrEP is safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding. The ARVs used for PrEP, TDF and TDF/FTC, are frequently used in combination with other ARVs for HIV treatment. The latest WHO systematic review suggests that there does not appear to be a safety-related rationale for disallowing or discontinuing PrEP during pregnancy and breastfeeding for HIV- negative women who are at continuing risk of HIV acquisition. • PrEP
